Dora Lush  

Introduction

The difficulties of evaluation research in the psychoanalytical field are well known and have been discussed at some length in a previous paper (Boston, 1989). In that paper a pilot project exploring a new method for assessing the results of psychoanalytical psychotherapy with children was outlined and we should like to share our experience of carrying out this project and to consider further implications for methodology.

Evaluation research has been defined as the activity of relating results to objectives (Fonagy and Higgitt, 1989). It is not at all easy, however, to define in any simple, researchable way the objectives of psychoanalytical work.

Jason: The Complex Elusiveness of Labelling

It can be useful when considering a particular concept to start by turning to the Oxford English Dictionary. In the present case, the word I looked up — ‘label’ — yielded unexpected results. I found nine entries under ‘label, substantive’. The first and root meaning is ‘a narrow band or strip of linen, cloth, etc.’ After a number of obsolete uses we get to its meaning in heraldry — ‘a mark of cadency distinguishing the eldest son of a family and consisting in a band drawn across the upper part of the shield …’ the first step in the transition in meaning to the word's current figurative sense. The chief current sense we find under entry 7: ‘A slip of paper, cardboard, metal etc. attached … to an object and bearing its name, description or destination. Lynda Ellis

Lynda Ellis

104 Thorne Road
Doncaster

Lynda Ellis  

Introduction

This paper attempts to address some of the difficulties and complexities which I have encountered in working with children caught in an enveloping and invasive relationship with mother such that on a number of levels they become indistinguishable one from the other. It borrows from the world of natural science the idea of diffusion, that is:

the random movement of substances from a region of high to a region of low concentration down a concentration gradient, the rate of movement is determined by how steep the gradient is and diffusion is more rapid where the relative difference in concentrations is large.

(Barker, 1988)

and applies it to other than physiological processes in an attempt to describe and understand the nature of the ‘psychic flow’ between three particular mother-child dyads.

Paul V. TradShort-term Parent—Infant Psychotherapy, New York: Basic Books, 1993, hardback, 350 pp.

Lisa Miller

Lisa Miller

Tavistock Clinic
120 Belsize Lane
London NW3 5BA

Lisa Miller  

Paul V. Trad, M.D. is the Director of the Child and Adolescent Outpatient Department at Cornell University Medical School and Editor-in-Chief of the American Journal of Psychotherapy. From this it can be gathered that his thinking is likely both to reflect current preoccupations in the field of child mental health and also to influence them.

391

Clearly, at present, there is much general enthusiasm for parent-infant psychotherapy; the idea of tackling disturbance at the roots, of fielding in close to the wicket, appeals powerfully to those influenced by the current coalescence of child development theory with psychoanalytic ideas. Many of us, strongly aware of the importance of earliest experiences, are seeking ways to alter the angle of development at the centre; the availability for family growth and change in the first months and years of a child's life has led us to see the value of not only early but also brief intervention. We are encouraged by the results of brief work with parents and infants, where attention to the parents’ infantile anxieties combined with an approach to their adult selves can join with attention to the infant to result in general progress and development, sometimes of a rapid sort.

Paul V. Trad is fired by theories of child development and in touch with psychodynamic issues. He concentrates mainly on the dyad, the mother-infant couple, and gives us long, detailed and lively case descriptions; this is particularly enlightening and valuable where he makes us think about mothers who are significantly ill and shows us the influence and benefit which containing attention has even in very anxiety-provoking cases.

The technique, or the idea, which the author is promoting is called ‘previewing’, the ‘process which adaptive caregivers seek to introduce their infants to imminent developmental change’. This phenomenon seems to connect with the idea which child psychotherapists here might have of a mother who is able to conceive of her baby as having a life of his or her own, a notion of the child's separateness from birth and a faith in the child's innate independent capacity which allows the parents not only to lead or to drive but also to follow the infant's development. Trad discusses issues like maternal fears aroused by the infant's developing autonomy and the mother's failure to reconcile her expectations of the baby with the reality of the experience. He finds that mothers in difficulties cannot ‘preview’: that is to say, they cannot look ahead and anticipate and move with their babies’ development.

On Seeing and Not Seeing1

Sylvia Wilson

Sylvia Wilson

41 Cavendish Place
Jesmond
Newcastle-upon-Tyne
NE2 2NE

Sylvia Wilson  

In her 1981 commemorative essay on Bion's theory of thinking, Edna O'Shaughnessy asks the question ‘What does Bion mean by “Thinking”?’ and continues:

He does not mean some abstract mental process. His concern is with thinking as a human link — the endeavour to understand, comprehend the reality of, get insight into the nature of … oneself and another. Thinking is an emotional experience of trying to know one's self and someone else.

(O'Shaughnessy, 1981: 181)

Endeavouring to understand the emotional impact of congenital blindness or severe visual impairment on the development of the child requires of me, as a sighted person, an imaginative leap into a world which is necessarily different from my own. I am bounded by the experience of my own vision. If I am to reach into the world of the visually impaired child I must both hold to the experience I know and accept the dignity of theirs.

The blind and severely visually impaired children I have encountered in my work over the last seventeen years have constantly challenged my thinking. While it is of course true that there are common patterns of development, no two children are alike.

165

‘If I bring up the sexual problems of the kids,’ says P., who teaches Shop in Junior High, ‘the others will say: “Stick to your woodwork!” This is the time for Socrates’ question — what is woodwork? The young man cannot hammer a nail because he does not hammer on the outbreath. He holds back his anger. We want our young people to have skill and strength, but we will not speak of aggression. We want the work to be beautiful, but we will not speak of sex.’

(Goodman, 1969)

In psychoanalysis we will speak of sex — but not as much as we used to. Perhaps we are getting on. Puberty, however, brings an urgency to matters of sex and sexuality that usually forces them to everyone's attention, unless interest and curiosity are made subject to the principle of the need not to know.

Editorial

Following the publication of the latest results of the Tavistock research on evaluation in the last issue of this Journal, it is a pleasure to publish for the wider readership a version of the paper given at the ACP conference in March of this year by the Great Ormond Street team. This paper outlines the research programme on sexually offending behaviour in young adolescent boys, focusing on the extended assessments (over twelve sessions) undertaken by the child psychotherapist team members. The vivid clinical material in Part II not only provides a thoughtful comment on the role, technique and focus of such brief work but also offers much preliminary thinking on the link between sexuality and violence.

Don Campbell draws on his experience at the Portman Clinic, London, in his article on assessment of adolescent sexual abusers. The importance and protection of the ‘ego ideal’ is stressed and many readers will be interested in his concept of ‘the shame shield’. It seems sometimes as if the concept of ‘shame’ has lost favour in the psychoanalytic world: perhaps a new debate can be opened.

With two opening papers on parallel themes, we have chosen to follow with a Jungian paper in which Jane Bunster delightfully traces her work with 6-year-old Louis as he negotiates the process of ‘de-integration’ — discovering his potential as a child able to encounter and meet the world, with a range of positive and negative feelings. The ‘good-enough’ experience is described, interwoven with material from infant observation to illuminate the thesis.

Abuse by the system is the theme of Debbie Hindle's paper ‘Learning to think in a war zone’.

281

[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

As this issue goes to press, we anticipate an interesting ACP conference on violence and children and look forward, in May, to the Athens conference of the EFPP on the theme of transference and countertransference. Readers who attend conferences and study-days around the world may like to keep the Journal in mind, encouraging authors to submit papers for consideration where they feel an area of interest to Journal readers has been elaborated. In this way we hope to enable a lively discussion and sharing of ideas across geographical and theoretical divides.

Having begun Volume 20 with the Special Issue on Autism, we continue the Journal year with a general issue. The papers cover a range of topics, including research, issues of motherhood and mothering, and clinical case studies.

We are delighted to publish the paper ‘Early aspects of mothering’ by Erna Furman, a member of our recently formed Advisory Board. Building on a lifetime of experience of working with mothers and their children, and elaborating on ideas from her many previous publications, Furman considers the various states of mind of mothers faced with separation from their child, either through bereavement or through the child's normal developmental process of individuation. The mother's emotional experiences of separation are explored in relation to bodily states and to the variety of defences used to cope with the sense of loss, and comparison is made between mothers’ and fathers’ experiences of the child's moves towards independence. This paper discusses the range from normality to pathology, and offers insight into some developmental aspects of mothering.

147

From Confusional Entanglement to Sense of Self: Aetiology, Thinking and Process in Work with an Autistic Boy

Carol Hughes

Carol Hughes

14 The Gardens
East Dulwich
London SE22

Carol Hughes  

Introduction

This paper arose from thinking about eighteen months of therapy with Dean, a latency autistic boy who, I felt, had begun to emerge as a clear personality from a muddled mass of confusion and autistic symptoms. As he issued from his state of psychic ‘confusional entanglement’ (Tustin, 1990), he could be seen to be developing an independent sense of himself and others.

In parallel, however, I found that I was less than clear about the concept of autism: somehow, the autistic disturbance is such that it is particularly difficult to conceptualize. Autistic children themselves seem to be in the grip of occurrences which appear to have little or no mental existence for them and in which their behaviour seems to carry no meaning at all. In my work with Dean this difficulty in thinking and in attributing meaning has been reflected both within the treatment itself and externally in the complex care network surrounding this child.

Autism: A Family Affair?1

Averil Earnshaw

Averil Earnshaw

13 Cawarrah Road
Middle Cove 2068
Sydney, Australia

Averil Earnshaw  

Introduction

This paper records some of my experiences of being with, and trying to understand, a small group of children who had already been diagnosed as autistic. I saw them in their special classes at school, and at home with their families. I make no claim to be presenting either a scientific investigation or any conclusions about autism. Reports of such studies are available in various scientific journals. However, I must record that my experiences with these children left me wondering if an autistic child really exists as a separate entity. No child in this group seemed to have a sense of self, of being an individual, of being aware of himself or herself as having a separate body, or a separate psyche.

My conceptual framework, as outlined in this paper, is based on my experiences of observing, feeling and thinking about what was going on, as I spent two years with these children. There are, of course, other conceptual frameworks from within which one can classify an autistic child's behaviour and from which management of the condition may be given. This very fact of multiplicity suggests that no one view of the cause, and no one way of treatment, has been effective.

It is therefore in the spirit of continuing enquiry that I offer my observations and experiences with this small group of children. Perhaps this record of my experiences will encourage others to be with these children and their families, and to explore further the possible meanings of the condition.

Viviane Green  

There is a particular pleasure in reading an autobiography where an interest in that strange country which is the past is married to a keen literary sensibility. This reflects Pontalis's interests: literature and psychoanalysis. His youth and adolescence were fuelled by a love of literature and in later life he became an analyst. His early interest was maintained by becoming a contributor to Sartre's influential journal Les Temps Modernes. He then became the editor of La Nouvelle Revue de Psychoanalyse, while also practising as an analyst.

As Adam Phillips points out in his introduction, Proust is everywhere in this book, which is as much about the process of the act of remembering through language as it is about the evocation of specific people, places and events. The book is an exploration, imbued with aphorisms and meditations on the intricate links between erstwhile, lived, sensuous experiences, of the nature of memory and language itself. The writer's self-confessed evolving love-hate relationship with his ‘anxious passion’, language, is the organizing thread and what captivated this reader.

A life, Pontalis reminds us, is irreducible to one narrative; a multiplicity of interpretations is possible. Language, the means of telling and structuring experience, is double-edged. It gives shape, order, definition and fixity to experience that was once spontaneous, vibrant and often silent. Thus, while language can convey memory, it is also that which can betray ‘the hollows’, moments of experiences such as dreaming, loving and loss. It is the moment when ‘time tables and the use of words and distribution of space all collapse. When words fail, it is because, without realizing it, one is about to touch a different earth.

Editorial

On behalf of the Editorial Committee, we are delighted to present the first issue of the Journal oífChild Psychotherapy to be published by Routledge. We hope that the change in format, size and design of ‘the little red book’ will meet with your approval and that the prospect of three issues per year will be pleasing. Our new colleagues at Routledge have proved sensitive to the needs, demands and occasional vagaries both of the committee and of our professional readership: we anticipate a creative liaison and value especially the business and marketing knowledge which Routledge bring to this venture.

The appointment of the Advisory Board represents a further step in the development of the Journal. It has been most rewarding to receive warm and welcoming letters from this distinguished group, applauding the move forward and offering support. We are delighted that they have joined us.

It is a particular honour to be able to publish in this new volume two papers which Frances Tustin intends to be her last. With typical generosity she has chosen this forum ‘to communicate my experience to my fellow child psychotherapists’. Mrs Tustin is an honorary member of the Association of Child Psychotherapists, an Honorary Affiliate of the British Psychoanalytic Society and a Corresponding Member of the Psychoanalytic Center of California. To many of us she is also a much-loved teacher, supervisor and friend, modest of person and intensely stimulating of curiosity and thought. The sadness that we may not receive her thinking in print again is tempered by this generous gift. It may be of interest to readers to know that Mrs Tustin's work will be included in a new series by Routledge of introductory critical texts entitled Makers of Modern Psychotherapy. The volume on Frances Tustin will be by Sheila Spensley.

Donald Campbell

Donald Campbell

8 Fitzjohns Avenue
London NW3 5NA

Donald Campbell  

Introduction

The Home Office reported in 1988 (HMSO, 1988) that one-third of all known sex offenders are adolescents. Bearing in mind that all sex crimes are significantly under-reported, it is disturbing that victim surveys in the US1 indicate that approximately 50 per cent of child molestations were committed by adolescents (Fehrenbach et al., 1986). The adolescents’ first sexual offences usually occurred between the ages of 12 and 15 (Deisher et al, 1982). It was estimated that the average adolescent sexual offender would during his lifetime commit 380 sexual crimes (Becker and Abel, 1984).

Puberty and the developmental phase of adolescence create internal conflicts which contribute to the adolescent's abusive behaviour. While sexually abusing offenders are caught up in the throes of adolescence, these internal conflicts may be more accessible to both the worker and the adolescent. In light of the fact that approximately half the adult sex offenders coming before the courts began their sexual deviancy in adolescence (Davis, 1987), one can see the enormous prophylactic potential in work with adolescent abusers.

Quoting these lines from ‘On first looking into Chapman's Homer’, Beta Copley states, ‘A love of literature may serve as a conveyor and container of discovery of a new world’ (p. 119). Many reading this book will feel that they are either discovering, or exploring with renewed excitement and insight, a very particular world — that of Adolescence. Deborah Hindle

Dorchester Road
Nottingham NG3 6LF

Deborah Hindle  

Bion equates the need for awareness of emotional experiences with truth and the lack of such awareness with deprivation of truth. ‘The effect on the personality of such deprivation is analogous to the effect of physical starvation on the physique’ (Bion, 1962).

This paper is about one 9-year-old boy's struggle to think and to understand the truth of his life in the midst of a prolonged legal dispute. He had been living with the same foster parents for five years and was already in twice weekly psychotherapy when his birth mother applied to the court for a revocation of the care order. Although this proceeding took place prior to the implementation of the Children Act 1989, it highlights some of the problems faced when a birth parent or parents apply to the court for access or custody of a child who has been in the care of the local authority for an extended period.

The Children Act places the best interests of the child as paramount but also emphasizes the responsibility of parents towards children and the need for local authorities to work in partnership with parents. The problem of maintaining stability for a child whose future is not secured by adoption and of facilitating meaningful contact with birth parents often involves a difficult balance. For Jamie, the length of the legal proceedings, the uncertainty of the situation and the increased access to his birth mother exposed him to what I have called a second dose of the original trauma of his early experiences.

Introduction

In my earlier article ‘Mothers have to be there to be left’ (1982), I described how important it is for the child's healthy growth that a mother remain fully available to him while supporting and appreciating his develop mentally self-initiated steps towards becoming a person in his own right. I stressed that this mutually crucial process in the mother—child relationship entails great emotional hardship for the mother. Taking weaning-to-self-feeding as a prototypical developmental step, I illustrated some common ways in which mothers unconsciously avoid or mitigate their distress at ‘being left’ at the cost of jeopardizing the child's mastery. I also listed several other developmental milestones, such as the child's entry into pre-school and latency, to show that this oft-repeated lifelong process remains difficult for mothers throughout and always tends to mobilize their defensive responses. Toddlers and Their Mothers (E. Furman, 1992a) provided much more extensive and detailed clinical data as well as a much deeper understanding of these developmental changes in the mother—child relationship, with special focus on the toddler's acquiring ownership of his body through self-care.

Deintegration: The Gate to Development

Jane Bunster

Jane Bunster

93 Tufnell Park Road
London, N7 0PS

Jane Bunster  

Introduction

The main thesis of this paper is concerned with the effect that a traumatic loss or series of losses may have on the physical and psychological development of children. I want to emphasize that feelings around loss, for example, the loss of the breast at weaning, loss of a parent or grandparent or other significant person, or moving house or schools, will be imbued with primitive infantile phantasies which need to be acknowledged, contained and transformed into thoughts. If these feelings cannot be contained by a reasonable environment, because of either trauma or an unavailable thinking caretaker/parent, it is likely that the child will feel totally overwhelmed and an unconscious defence pattern will develop to protect him, and also his loved objects. The extreme defence against an impinging environment, either external or internal, may result in autistic states of mind or in psychosomatic symptoms where unacceptable thoughts are transmuted into bodily symptoms. It is as though there is no gateway through which these difficult feelings can pass and be thought about, thus impeding psychological and physical development.

Christopher Reeves

Christopher Reeves

Christopher Reeves  

Sayers’ book is a comparative study of the work of four female psychoanalytic pioneers: Helene Deutsch, Karen Horney, Anna Freud and Melanie Klein. Her theme is that the origins and early development of psychoanalysis were dominated by a male perspective on human development. This perspective stemmed from Freud, whose masculine identity was reinforced by the male dominance and prejudices of the society in which he grew up, and these in turn were bolstered and rationalized rather than challenged by his theoretical formulations. The result, according to the author, was the establishment of a ‘patriarchal and phallocentric’ theory and therapy, which has since given way to one ‘which is now almost entirely mother-centred’. Her chosen quartet of female psychoanalysts are seen as having played a crucial role in bringing this about.

Undoubtedly, there has been a shift of focus in psychoanalysis during the past half century both in the predominant types of presenting symptoms, from Oedipal and post-Oedipal to pre-Oedipal conditions, and towards a more maternal conception of the analyst's role (or at least one less exclusively father-centred than that habitually adopted by Freud). The question is, what part did these four women pioneers play in these developments? Were they, as the author suggests, each in their own way ‘architects of this revolution’? Or is her whole argument misconceived?

There are a number of different levels on which the author argues her case.

Sylvia Wilson  

Understanding Your Handicapped Child is a small, slim, 80-page volume of clear, large print and it has the strength of simplicity in both style and presentation, while being about a complex and difficult subject.

It is, as the title suggests, directed towards parents who have the difficult emotional and practical task of bringing up a child who suffers

393

from a disability and therefore faces not only the ordinary traumas and vulnerability of life that confront each one of us but also an increased vulnerability in a not always sympathetic world. In the introduction, the author says,

Parents have hopes and plans for each child, that, on the whole, are properly suited to them — whatever their difficulties and strengths. This book is to help you be in even more touch with your child's unique problems and potential.

If you have a child with a handicap or disability, this book is intended to strengthen your ability to deal with the emotional experiences involved. You are not alone however much it feels like that.

Valerie Sinason never strays from placing disability within the context of normality, that is the context of normal, universal human experience, which can be, might have to be, and perhaps unconsciously is, faced by each one of us ‘regardless of race, religion, class, economic or educational position’. The sense of particularity and the attempt to address special and unique needs while at the same time normalizing those is strengthened by the fact that this book appears in a series of well-presented, short and accessible books for parents on understanding children at differing stages of development.

The voice of the author is sensitive, hopeful and helpfully authoritative and the book carries with it a real attempt to provide, at many levels. Within the text she intelligently and practically informs the reader with meaningful statistics. She cites the facts that ‘Within the United Kingdom there are 360,000 children born with disabilities. In the world, over 1% of all new babies born will have some kind of disability’ and ‘Out of approximately 8 million people in Britain with hearing disabilities only 55,000 have British Sign Language’ (p. 54), and thus touches on the political as well as the personal responsibilities we all share. She includes a list of organizations and positive projects which can help and in this way maintains the balance between practical support and compassionate understanding that parents need.

This paper is an attempt to sort out my ideas about autism before my professional life comes to an end. It is fitting that I should do this with the Association of Child Psychotherapists because, as you will see, I have been very helped in my thinking by child psychotherapy colleagues of various theoretical persuasions.

I should like to think about an error made by many psychoanalytic therapists (including myself), to which I drew attention in a paper published in The International Journal of Psycho-Analysis as recently as 1991. In that paper I pointed out that observational studies of babies by workers from many countries — such as Colwyn Trevarthen (1979) in Scotland; Daniel Stern (1983, 1985) in the United States; Miller, Rustin and Shuttleworth in England (1989); Piontelli (1992) in Italy; Perez-Sanchez (1990) in Spain — had shown conclusively that there is not a normal infantile stage of primary autism to which the pathology of childhood autism could be a regression. This has been the mainstream hypothesis concerning the aetiology of childhood autism to which many psychoanalytic therapists have subscribed, especially in the United States and in Europe. This flawed hypothesis, based on faulty premises, has been like an invasive virus in that it has permeated and distorted clinical and theoretical formulations. It has perpetuated these distortions and obstructed communication between psychodynamic workers with autistic children. It has also obstructed communication with our Jungian colleagues, for example with Dr Michael Fordham, whose model is of a ‘primary self’ that innately unfolds (or not, as in autism)

Introduction

Radio and television programmes in England about childhood autism invariably imply that autistic children are inevitably brain damaged. This has not been my experience. All the autistic children I treated by psychotherapy had all been carefully investigated organically. They were found to have no brain damage by the investigative methods then available. (All but one were seen at Great Ormond Street Children's Hospital and were diagnosed as ‘autistic’ by the late Dr Mildred Creak who had an international reputation as a diagnostician of childhood psychosis.)

Autistic Breathing

Maria Rhode

Maria Rhode

28 Holland Park
London W11 3TA

Maria Rhode  

The history of many autistic children shows a severe disruption occurring around the time of birth. This may take the form of actual physical difficulties at birth that the child has not been able to recover from; of depression in the mother; of hostility aroused in the parents by the particular child or what it represents (which may include their lack of permission from their own internal objects to have a healthy child); or of damage of various kinds to the child which serves to traumatize the parents so that they are not able to attend to the child they have. It can seem as though the family had been literally ‘winded’ by the arrival of this particular baby. (Of course, not all autistic children's history shows this particular pattern: the autism may be the reaction to a later trauma in which it seemed that the child's own destructiveness had been actualized in external reality. Such a case has been described by Velleda Cecchi (Cecchi, 1990), although even here the trauma of political events was preceded by depression on the part of the child's mother.) In Frances Tustin's terms, the child has experienced psychological — and sometimes physical — birth as a catastrophe (Tustin, 1992: 96ff.).

I wish to discuss material from two autistic children which relates to the two major physical changes undergone at birth, that is, to the cutting of the cord and the onset of breathing. One of these children was reported to have had difficulties in beginning to breathe, although not sufficiently dramatic ones to have left a clear memory in his parents’ minds. No physical distress at birth was reported in the other's case, but his parents had been given cause to worry about his development in utero

Live Company is a beautifully written, carefully documented exposition of thirty years’ intensive psychoanalytic work by a highly accomplished child psychotherapist. In a modest way, sparing the reader none of the ‘horror, disbelief and boredom’ of this work, Alvarez describes her heroic efforts to reclaim ‘greenesse’ in the ‘shrivelled hearts’ of hopeless children — children who to all intents and purposes have become dead to the world. Some are autistic, others live on the tenuous border between sanity and madness; some have grown up in nice caring households, others have suffered gross injustices and indignities through abuse and deprivation.

There are sixteen chapters which take us through the ups and downs of treatment, charting the progress and regress of her patients, as well as the pathways and blind alleys of Alvarez’ personal analytic development. With unusual candour, Alvarez tells us about the psychoanalytic concepts which have helped as well as those which may have hindered her understanding. Where the language of psychoanalysis falls short, Alvarez turns to literature and to developmental psychology. For the psychoanalytic reader who enjoys the wider culture, the book is unusually imaginative as well as informative.

From the first chapter, ‘The long fall’, to the final chapter on the use of countertransference in relation to the ‘Rites and rituals of autism’, we follow Alvarez’ work with Robbie, an autistic boy who started treatment at age 4 and is now an adult of 30.

Case History of Farida: A Year of Psychotherapy with a Girl Who Said She Was Sexually Abused

Sheena Grünberg

Sheena Grünberg

Denmark Hill
London SE5 8AZ

Sheena Grünberg  

This is the story of a girl whom I shall call Farida, who said she was sexually abused. The aim of this paper is to explore, on the basis of three times weekly psychotherapy, her ways of thinking, using Bion's theory of thinking to assess whether this allegation is likely to be true or false. Or, whether true or false, if the disclosure so blinded the carers that further mistreatment took place because of failure to understand the real communication underneath.

History

Farida, an Asian girl, was originally referred when she was 12 years old, by her present foster-parents, because she appeared depressed and inconsolably unhappy. A brief outline of her previous history is that Farida's mother died when she was 3 years old and her brother, whom I shall call Imran, was 1 year old.
